newsitem.title: PERU: Peru waits for next round of hostage crisis talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru waits for next round of hostage crisis talks.

text.p: Peru waited on Friday for the next round of face-to-face negotiations between a crisis-weary government and defiant Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages for the 59th day as bargaining chips to free jailed comrades.

President Alberto Fujimori's administration announced another meeting with the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) was scheduled to take place by Saturday afternoon, but did not give more details.

A first formal meeting on Tuesday between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA No. 2 Rolly Rojas, alias "The Arab," produced a pledge for further talks but little more apparent progress in the aim for a peaceful solution.

Speaking publicly about the meeting for the first time late on Thursday, Palermo described it as "absolutely normal" and "quite positive." He added "we are going to continue our work, and then we hope to have results", but also warned "we are very worried" about the situation in general.
With a pact of silence by all sides on the details of the negotiations, local media speculated feverishly about what progress may or may not have been made.

Local weekly magazine Caretas, without naming its sources, said Rojas had made three demands on the rebels' behalf for the freedom of some 400 imprisoned MRTA members, safe passage by plane to Peru's central jungle with 15 hostages as temporary guarantors, and an improvement in prison conditions.
"Palermo was cautious. He said they knew that the government's position on the prisoners was fixed and that it coincided with public national and international opinion," Caretas said.

The government's refusal to consider the MRTA's central demand for releases had stalled efforts to set up a formal talks' process since Palermo entered the residence to meet rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini on Dec. 28.

Fujimori and his Cabinet spent Thursday mapping out strategy. Fresh from a four-day trip to London, Fujimori met for three hours with his ministers to be debriefed on latest developments and plan next moves in a crisis that has become his worst dilemma in six turbulent years in office.

After weeks of deadlock, this week's resumption of dialogue, in a safe house across the street from the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence where the MRTA stormed a cocktail party last Dec. 17, marked a breakthrough.
But with the rebels refusing to give up their demand for releases, and the government flatly rejecting that, a peaceful end is not expected soon.
The next talks will take place in the same house, rented by the Red Cross, who used a metal detector on Tuesday to ensure no one entered with weapons.

Holed up in the envoy's mansion for more than eight weeks, the hostages are showing deepening signs of physical and mental strain. The Red Cross, which is both mediating in the crisis and providing humanitarian aid, has stepped up medical activities inside the compound in recent days.

The organisation laid cables on Thursday to carry electricity into the fortified embassy residence for the first time since the early days of the siege when the government cut services. Three specialist doctors used the electricity for heart monitoring equipment they took into the building.

The last two hostages released from the compound have been freed on medical grounds and relatives claim several remaining captives are seriously ill. Aid workers and police say many hostages are being treated for ailments such as hypertension, digestive problems or depression.

Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer said the health of Judge Moises Pantoja, who wrote to his family complaining of arthritic pain, and legislator Gilberto Siura, being treated for cancer, was "delicate."
The minister added, however, that the health of the captives in general was "good" under the circumstances, "and the dangerous cases are controlled."
Both sides have sought to avoid harming the hostages, but Fujimori has warned he will rule out using force to end the siege only while all the hostages remain unharmed.

The remaining hostages include Fujimori's brother and a brother-in-law, two government ministers, a handful of top security force and judicial officials, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia and about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
